analysis.investment_thesis: Aakaar Medical fails the Magic Formula on the critical dimension — return on capital is essentially zero (ROE 0.34%), signaling the business earns almost nothing on deployed capital. Even at a P/E of 11.9, a business that cannot compound capital is not "cheap and good" — it's just mediocre and fragile.
key_strengths: P/E of 11.90 implies ~8.4% earnings yield — adequate but not bargain territory
High promoter holding of 67.05% signals skin in the game
Operates in the structurally growing aesthetic/personal care niche
key_risks: ROE of 0.34% is near-zero — capital is not earning returns
Tiny INR 71.7 Cr market cap — illiquid SME with limited financial visibility
No FII participation (0%) — institutional validation absent
red_flags: ROE of 0.34% is a severe Magic Formula disqualifier — ROIC is almost certainly well below my 20% threshold
Positive P/E with near-zero ROE suggests unsustainably thin earnings base — one bad quarter turns EBIT negative
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula demands two things simultaneously: a high earnings yield (cheap) and a high return on capital (good business). Aakaar scores poorly on the more important of the two. A 0.34% ROE means for every ₹100 of equity, the company earns 34 paise — this is not a business that compounds capital, it's a business that barely breaks even on its asset base. No matter how cheap the stock becomes, a company earning sub-1% on capital destroys shareholder value versus even a risk-free government bond yielding 7%+.

The 8.4% earnings yield (inverse of P/E 11.9) is not compensation enough for the absence of return-on-capital quality. In my framework, I would much rather pay a 6% earnings yield for a 30% ROIC business than an 8% yield for a 0.3% ROE business. The combination of micro-cap size (₹71.7 Cr), zero FII interest, and negligible profitability makes this a clear avoid on systematic quantitative grounds. This is precisely the kind of name the Magic Formula screen filters out.
